x: Under the income method GDP (domestic product) is the sum of factor incomes earned within the domestic territory (wages, rent, interest, profit, mixed income), with depreciation added for the gross figure; adding NFIA gives a national, not domestic, aggregate. Transfer payments are never part of factor incomes, so 'minus transfer payments' is not a step of the method.
source: NextGen Indian Economy - APPSC 12 p.3-5; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy 10th ed. part 03 p.47
evidence: NCERT Class 12 Macroeconomics ch.2 (income method: GDP = W + P + In + R)
old notes 3:22 sub 0 (copied the printed key)
dispute: Printed key and old notes: domestic factor incomes minus transfer payments. Strictly: GDP by the income method = sum of domestic factor incomes; transfers are simply excluded (NCERT Class 12 Macroeconomics ch.2).

x: Pearson's empirical relation is Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean, usually written Mode − Mean = 3(Median − Mean) (option 4, the key). Option 3 (Mode − Median = 2(Median − Mean)) is the same identity rearranged, so it is also algebraically true; options 1 and 2 are false.
source: Pearson's empirical relation (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness: Pearson mode and median skewness coefficients, (mean − mode)/s ≈ 3(mean − median)/s); algebra checked
evidence: algebra: Mode = 3Md − 2M ⇒ Mode − Md = 2(Md − M) and Mode − M = 3(Md − M)
dispute: Key / books: Mode − Mean = 3(Median − Mean) (the standard form). Strictly option 3 (Mode − Median = 2(Median − Mean)) is the same identity rearranged and also true.

x: The chi-square distribution is asymmetric: it is skewed to the right (positively skewed) and becomes nearly symmetric only for large degrees of freedom. Option 1 is the key, and option 3 says the same thing more precisely.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chi-squared_distribution (skewness √(8/k) > 0, tends to symmetry as k grows)
dispute: Key: asymmetric. More precisely: positively (right) skewed (option 3), which is also true (Wikipedia Chi-squared distribution).
